name: HelenOS
summary: Free general-purpose operating system designed from scratch around the modular SPARTAN microkernel, running its drivers and services in user space with exceptional portability across eight processor architectures.

content.introduction: HelenOS is a free general-purpose operating system written entirely from scratch in the C language. Initiated in 2001 by Jakub Jermář at the Faculty of Mathematics and Physics of Charles University in Prague, the project has grown into an international collaborative research initiative. HelenOS aims to explore the design of a modern and robust operating system founded on a genuine **multi-server microkernel** architecture, in which each classic function (hardware drivers, file systems, network stack, display management) is moved into independent and isolated processes running in user space, without reproducing the historical constraints or the monolithic complexity of Unix systems.
content.what_is_it: Technically, HelenOS is neither a Linux derivative nor a Unix clone: it is a stand-alone system implementing its own native abstractions. Its privileged ring 0 kernel, named SPARTAN, is strictly limited to the essential primitive features: preemptive scheduling of threads within tasks, paged virtual memory management and inter-process message switching (IPC). Almost all the services of the system, the device manager (devman), the service location server (locsrv), the virtual file system server (vfs) and all the drivers, run in user space (Ring 3) as unprivileged tasks.
content.spartan_microkernel_and_asynchronous_ipc: The architecture of the SPARTAN microkernel guarantees high operational resilience: the unforeseen failure or the crash of a disk driver, of a network interface or of a file system manager causes no kernel panic. The faulty component can be isolated, stopped and restarted by the service supervisor without interrupting the execution of the rest of the machine. Inter-process communications rest on a native asynchronous IPC protocol based on messages with four integer arguments, complemented by virtual memory sharing for transfers of large volumes of data.
content.filesystems_storage_and_network_stack: HelenOS integrates a virtual file system server (VFS) moved into user space which unifies access to data. The system supports a wide variety of storage formats: the FAT family (FAT12, FAT16, FAT32), ext4 (basic reading and writing), exFAT, ISO 9660 (optical disks), UDF and Minix FS. The network stack is also modular and decomposed into several cooperative daemons supporting Ethernet, the IP layer (IPv4 and experimental IPv6), the TCP and UDP transport protocols, as well as basic utilities (DHCP client, DNS resolver, download tool).
content.user_interface_bdsh_and_graphical_compos: To interact with the user, HelenOS has two distinct environments: an interactive text-mode command interpreter named **bdsh** (Brain Dead Shell), equipped with process inspection utilities, console text editors and diagnostic tools; and a native windowed graphical environment in user space (**ui** / display server). The latter offers a window manager with title bars, interaction buttons, vector and bitmap font rendering, a windowed graphical terminal emulator as well as lightweight demonstration games.
content.exceptional_multi_architecture_portabili: The most remarkable technical achievement of HelenOS is its native portability across eight different processor families: **IA-32** (32-bit x86), **AMD64** (x86-64), **ARM** (ARMv4 to ARMv7, Raspberry Pi), **AArch64** (64-bit ARM), **MIPS** (MIPS32 and MIPS64, Malta and PlayStation 2 platforms), **PowerPC** (32-bit), **SPARC V9** (UltraSPARC), and **RISC-V** (RV64). Distributed under the free and permissive **3-Clause BSD Licence**, HelenOS runs optimally within hypervisors (QEMU) and on compatible physical machines, constituting an academic research platform of great value.
content.versions_publiees_et_cibles_materielles: The most recent published version is HelenOS 0.14.1. For each version, the project publishes the release notes, the source archives and binary images classified by architecture and by machine. 0.14.1 covers amd64 (generic PC, ISO image), arm32 (BeagleBoard XM, BeagleBone, GTA02, IntegratorCP, Raspberry Pi), arm64 (HiKey960 and QEMU virt as ISO), ia32 (generic PC, ISO), ia64 (PowerEdge 3250/7250 and ski), mips32 (Malta in big and little endian, msim), ppc32 (G4 workstation, ISO) and sparc64 (Sun Ultra 5/60 and Sun Fire T1000, ISO). Nightly builds are available on the continuous integration infrastructure of the project, which makes it possible to follow the state of the repository between two versions. The download page lists only complete images, sources and release notes: no separately installable package appears there.
advantages: Pure and elegant multi-server microkernel architecture eliminating the risks of overall system crash.
All hardware drivers, file systems and network stacks run in isolated user space (Ring 3).
Exceptional multi-architecture portability covering eight processor families (x86, ARM, RISC-V, MIPS, PowerPC, SPARC).
Broad file system support (FAT12/16/32, ext4, exFAT, ISO 9660, Minix FS).
Complete environment including a command-line shell (bdsh) and a native windowed graphical server.
Source code of high academic quality, fully open under the free permissive 3-Clause BSD licence.
disadvantages: System designed primarily for academic research, with no claim to replace an industrial production system.
Restricted application catalogue compared with the software ecosystems of Linux or BSD distributions.
Absence of modern hardware support for contemporary Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and 3D acceleration of recent GPUs.
IPC communication overheads inherent to microkernel architectures under intense input/output demands.
Incompatibility with closed application ecosystems or native Linux containers.
who_is_it_for: Researchers, teachers and students in computing exploring the design of microkernels and multi-server systems.
System developers wishing to study a readable, clean and modular C language code base.
Embedded systems and hardware computing engineers targeting varied architectures (ARM, RISC-V, MIPS, SPARC).
Enthusiasts of alternative software architectures experimenting with new systems under QEMU.
who_is_it_not_for: General public users looking for an operating system for modern web browsing or video gaming.
Enterprises looking for certified environments for hosting servers with guaranteed commercial support.
Developers depending on closed proprietary software or high-level frameworks (Node.js, Electron, JVM).
Production infrastructures requiring massive deployments of heavy distributed databases.
content.verdict: HelenOS is an academic and technical project in the field of operating systems. By materialising the concept of a multi-server system in which each service and driver is confined to user space above the SPARTAN microkernel, and by ensuring portability across eight processor architectures, it constitutes an educational support for the study of systems.
